page.title: Advanced Gerund and Infinitive Patterns
page.subtitle_html: Advanced Gerund and Infinitive Patterns — B2 gerund and infinitive choices after verbs, adjectives, prepositions, and meaning-changing verbs.
page.subtitle_text: B2 gerund and infinitive choices after verbs, adjectives, prepositions, and meaning-changing verbs.

blocks.body: {"level":"B2","intro":"Advanced Gerund and Infinitive Patterns: Advanced Gerund and Infinitive Patterns focuses on B2 verb patterns where -ing and to-infinitive choices affect structure or meaning.","rules":[{"label":"Verb pattern","text":"Learn the verb together with the form that follows it.","example":"avoid doing / decide to do"},{"label":"Meaning change","text":"Some verbs change meaning with gerund or infinitive.","example":"remember locking / remember to lock"},{"label":"After prepositions","text":"After prepositions, use a gerund form.","example":"interested in learning"}]}

page.title: Complex Relative Clauses
page.subtitle_html: Complex Relative Clauses - C1 relative clauses with whose, prepositions, embedded information, and non-defining detail.
page.subtitle_text: C1 relative clauses with whose, prepositions, embedded information, and non-defining detail.

blocks.body: {"level":"C1","intro":"Complex Relative Clauses: compact anchors for precise C1 relative clauses.","rules":[{"label":"Whose","text":"Use whose to connect ownership or relationship without repeating the noun.","example":"The company whose reputation had suffered issued an apology."},{"label":"Prepositions","text":"In formal style, a preposition can stand before whom or which.","example":"The issue about which we disagreed has been resolved."},{"label":"Non-defining detail","text":"Use commas when the clause adds extra, non-essential information.","example":"The proposal, which many experts supported, was approved."}]}

page.title: Inversion After Negative Adverbials
page.subtitle_html: Inversion After Negative Adverbials - C1 fronted negative and limiting adverbials with auxiliary inversion.
page.subtitle_text: C1 fronted negative and limiting adverbials with auxiliary inversion.

blocks.body: {"level":"C1","intro":"Inversion After Negative Adverbials: compact C1 anchors for never, rarely, hardly, no sooner, not only, and only then.","rules":[{"label":"Negative adverbials","text":"After never, rarely, and seldom at the front, use auxiliary inversion.","example":"Never have I seen such a result."},{"label":"Hardly and no sooner","text":"Use past perfect inversion before when or than.","example":"No sooner had they left than the phone rang."},{"label":"Limiting expressions","text":"Use inversion after not only, under no circumstances, at no time, only then, and only after.","example":"Only then did I realize the mistake."}]}
